extracted.intended_audience: Iowa State students, Greenlee School community, and the general public interested in satire, headline writing, and First Amendment issues
extracted.subtask_short: writing satirical headlines for The Onion
extracted.subtask_description: Insights into how The Onion generates, selects, and edits satirical headlines and the editorial/legal considerations that shape those choices. Includes writers' room processes, headline types that tend to succeed, and the head writer's leadership role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate reader comprehension and laugh response
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines should replicate how readers experience a headline — they should either be immediately understood and provoke a laugh or be confusing (which is a failure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the writers' room writers read headlines aloud and the room immediately votes on each one to determine whether it moves on; Gillis notes 'the two main sounds in the writers’ room are laughter sometimes and, most of the time, just soul-crushing silence, in which you feel like you’ve failed completely at your job.' Use the room's instant reaction as a proxy for real-world reader response.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘3 a.m. deranged’ / surreal headline quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the best headlines 'defy any kind of logic' and are like '3 a.m. deranged headlines' — surreal, dreamlike, or absurd ideas rendered as straight news-style headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: 'Washington’s Hobby Lobby Lobbies To Strengthen Hobbies' (with sub-head) and 'Climate Protesters Terrified After Mona Lisa Extends Big Tongue And Starts Licking Up Soup.' These headlines work by embracing derangement/surreal imagery rather than literal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-volume ideation and aggressive editorial narrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Onion generates very large quantities of headline ideas and then aggressively narrows them down to what gets published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gillis describes starting with '1,500 or 2,000 headlines per week' and narrowing to the '40-50 headlines that ultimately get published.' This implies tolerance for broad ideation, iterating, and a gatekeeping editorial process that values only a small fraction of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of distinct meeting types: timely vs evergreen
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial meetings are split into 'timely meetings' for pressing news and 'evergreen meetings' for constant/worldwide topics, each serving a different purpose in headline selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely meetings address breaking or current news; evergreen meetings address perennial topics (example cited: 'the Midwestern rest-stop predicament'). Organize ideation sessions according to topic temporality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers' room mechanics: read-aloud, voting, and discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical mechanics of selection involve writers reading headlines aloud, immediate voting, and group discussion to decide what advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The read-aloud + vote system is used to quickly filter ideas: a headline is heard and the room votes to determine whether it moves on to further discussion. This process is explicitly used to simulate reader experience and filter for immediacy of comedic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head writer duties: editorial leadership, vision, and mediation
rubrics_metrics.description: The head writer role combines writing duties with editing others, developing a broader vision for the publication, and mediating among writer sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gillis describes responsibilities: generating headlines and articles, editing other writers’ drafts, developing where The Onion will go, and serving 'more of a mediator in the writers’ room.' Emphasizes accommodating contributors' sensibilities to bring out the best work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical stance: mockery and playing with facts instead of issuing grand statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the best satirical response is to highlight the absurdity of a situation rather than to craft a strong policy critique or sweeping statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gillis: when issues are 'so big and intractable, the best response can be saying “this is ridiculous” and making fun of the situation.' The approach is often to 'play around with the facts on the ground' rather than propose solutions or striking criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on legal protections (parody law and fair use) for satirical publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing satire depends on legal doctrines that protect parody and fair use, which enable The Onion to publish certain jokes without constant legal fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gillis states: 'we wouldn’t be able to publish funny, interesting jokes without parody law protections and fair use protections.' This signals that editorial decisions and risk assessments should account for parody/fair use boundaries and that legal safeguards are fundamental to enabling certain comedic targets or formats.
